title: CBSE Class 10 Social Science · Practice paper 2
subject: Social Science
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper contains 38 questions. All questions are compulsory.

The question paper has four sections of 20 marks each:
Section A: History, questions 1 to 9
Section B: Geography, questions 10 to 19
Section C: Political Science, questions 20 to 28
Section D: Economics, questions 29 to 38
Multiple choice questions (MCQs), including assertion-reason questions, carry 1 mark each.
Very Short Answer type questions (VSA) carry 2 marks each. Answers should not exceed 40 words.
Short Answer type questions (SA) carry 3 marks each. Answers should not exceed 60 words.
Long Answer type questions (LA) carry 5 marks each. Answers should not exceed 120 words.
Case-based questions (CBQ) carry 4 marks each and have three sub-questions. Answers should not exceed 100 words.

The map-based questions carry 5 marks: Q9 in Section A (2 marks) and Q19 in Section B (3 marks). Answers cannot be marked on a map here, so these questions use the text-based form that the CBSE Sample Question Paper gives for visually impaired candidates, with the same marks.
Write the answers of each section in that section only. Do not mix the answers of one section with another.
Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Why did the Roman Catholic Church begin to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558?
options: To fix the prices of printed books sold in Europe
To encourage the printing of the Bible in local languages
To control the spread of printed ideas that questioned its beliefs
To support the printing of Protestant writings
questions.sol: Printed books and tracts spread new readings of faith that the Church saw as heresy (for example, Menocchio's ideas). To curb such ideas, the Church imposed controls over publishers and booksellers and began the Index of Prohibited Books in 1558.
questions.chapter: History: Print Culture and the Modern World

Which of the following options is the correct match?
Column I (Person)Column II (Role)
1. Giuseppe MazziniX. Organised funds and went to fight in the Greek War of Independence
2. Lord ByronY. Founded the secret society Young Italy
3. Otto von BismarckZ. Chief minister of Prussia who led the unification of Germany
Choose the correct option:
questions.sol: Mazzini founded Young Italy in Marseilles; the English poet Lord Byron organised funds and went to fight in the Greek war, where he died of fever in 1824; Bismarck, the Prussian chief minister, was the architect of German unification.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Arrange the following events in chronological order, from the earliest to the latest:
I. Arrival of the Simon Commission in India
II. Massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar
III. Signing of the Poona Pact
IV. Violent clash at Chauri Chaura
Choose the correct option:
questions.sol: Jallianwala Bagh: 13 April 1919 (II); Chauri Chaura: February 1922 (IV); arrival of the Simon Commission: 1928 (I); Poona Pact: September 1932 (III).

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: In the pre-modern world, which of the following gradually moved the centre of world trade westwards and made Europe its centre?
options: The opening of the silk routes by European traders
The decline in the importance of the Americas
A ban on foreign trade by the rulers of India
China's reduced role in world trade and the rising importance of the Americas
questions.sol: Until well into the eighteenth century, China and India were among the richest countries. But from the fifteenth century China restricted its overseas contacts. China's reduced role and the rising importance of the Americas moved the centre of world trade westwards to Europe.
questions.chapter: History: The Making of a Global World

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain two effects of the introduction of the potato in Europe.
questions.model:
1. Europe's poor began to eat better and live longer once the humble potato became part of their diet.
2. Ireland's poorest peasants became so dependent on potatoes that when disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation. In the Great Irish Potato Famine (1845-1849), around 1,000,000 people died of starvation and about double that number emigrated in search of work.

points.t: The poor in Europe ate better and lived longer
Heavy dependence on potatoes in Ireland led to famine, deaths and emigration when the crop was destroyed by disease (1845-1849)

questions.chapter: History: The Making of a Global World

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: How did women in India become readers and writers with the growth of print in the nineteenth century? Explain with three examples.
questions.model:
1. Liberal husbands and fathers began educating their womenfolk at home, and sent them to schools when women's schools were set up in the cities after the mid-nineteenth century. Many journals carried writings by women and explained why women should be educated.
2. Rashsundari Debi, a young married girl in a very orthodox household, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen. Later she wrote her autobiography, Amar Jiban, published in 1876, the first full-length autobiography in the Bengali language.
3. From the 1860s, a few Bengali women such as Kailashbashini Debi wrote books highlighting the experiences of women: how they were imprisoned at home, kept in ignorance and forced to do hard domestic labour.
4. In the 1880s, in present-day Maharashtra, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai wrote with passionate anger about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows.

points.t: First example, e.g. women educated at home and in new women's schools; journals carried women's writings
Second example, e.g. Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly and wrote Amar Jiban (1876)
Third example, e.g. Kailashbashini Debi, or Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai writing about the lives of women and widows

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Describe how the peasants of Awadh and the tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills in Andhra Pradesh took part in the Non-Cooperation Movement. How did their idea of swaraj differ from that of the Congress? (2 + 2 + 1 = 5)
questions.model:
Awadh:
1. The peasants, led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been an indentured labourer in Fiji, struggled against talukdars and landlords who demanded very high rents and other cesses and forced them to do begar.
2. They demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and social boycott of oppressive landlords; panchayats organised nai-dhobi bandhs. The Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up in October 1920, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and others. In 1921, the houses of talukdars and merchants were attacked, bazaars were looted and grain hoards taken over.
Gudem Hills:
3. In the early 1920s a militant guerrilla movement spread here. The government had closed large forest areas, stopping people from grazing cattle and collecting fuelwood and fruits, and forced them to do begar for road building.
4. Led by Alluri Sitaram Raju, who spoke of Gandhiji's greatness but believed India could be freed only by force, the rebels attacked police stations, tried to kill British officials and carried on guerrilla warfare. Raju was captured and executed in 1924.
Idea of swaraj:
5. Each group gave swaraj its own meaning. For the Awadh peasants it meant freedom from oppressive landlords and begar; for the tribals it meant the right to enter forests and use their resources freely. Many used violent methods, while the Congress wanted a non-violent struggle for self-rule.

points.t: Awadh: Baba Ramchandra led peasants against talukdars and landlords over high rents, cesses and begar
Awadh: methods, e.g. nai-dhobi bandhs, Oudh Kisan Sabha (October 1920), or attacks on houses of talukdars and looting of bazaars in 1921
Gudem Hills: anger over closure of forests and forced begar for road building
Gudem Hills: guerrilla movement under Alluri Sitaram Raju; attacks on police stations; Raju executed in 1924
Swaraj meant freedom from local oppression (landlords, forest laws) to them, often by force, unlike the non-violent swaraj of the Congress

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Read the following text and answer the questions that follow:
The Frankfurt Parliament
In 1848, many political associations in the German regions, whose members were middle-class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans, met in the city of Frankfurt and decided to elect an all-German National Assembly. In May 1848, 831 elected representatives took their seats in the Church of St Paul. They drafted a constitution for a German nation that would be headed by a monarchy answerable to a parliament. The deputies offered the crown on these terms to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, the King of Prussia, but he refused it and joined other monarchs in opposing the elected assembly. The aristocracy and the army grew stronger in their opposition. The parliament was dominated by the middle classes, who resisted the demands of workers and artisans and so lost their support. Women were admitted only as observers in the visitors' gallery. In the end, troops were called in and the assembly was forced to break up.

parts.q: 8.1 Who refused the crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament?
parts.model: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, the King of Prussia.

points.t: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia

parts.q: 8.2 Why did the Frankfurt Parliament lose the support of workers and artisans?
parts.model: It was dominated by the middle classes, who resisted the demands of workers and artisans.

points.t: The middle classes who dominated it resisted the demands of workers and artisans

parts.q: 8.3 The liberal movements of 1848 were suppressed, yet the old order could not be fully restored. Evaluate two changes that took place in Central and Eastern Europe after 1848.
parts.model:
Monarchs began to realise that the cycles of revolution and repression could be ended only by granting concessions to the liberal-nationalist revolutionaries. So, after 1848, the autocratic monarchies of Central and Eastern Europe introduced changes that had already taken place in Western Europe before 1815:
1. Serfdom and bonded labour were abolished both in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia.
2. The Habsburg rulers granted more autonomy to the Hungarians in 1867.

points.t: First change: serfdom and bonded labour abolished in the Habsburg dominions and Russia
Second change: more autonomy granted to the Hungarians by the Habsburg rulers (1867), or a correct statement that monarchs granted concessions to end the cycle of revolution and repression

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Village ponds, public parks, picnic spots and grazing grounds that are open to all the people of a village are examples of:
questions.sol: Resources accessible to all the members of a community, such as village commons (grazing grounds, burial grounds, village ponds) and public parks and picnic spots in urban areas, are community owned resources.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Villagers near the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan have fought against mining by citing which law?
questions.sol: In the Sariska Tiger Reserve, villagers fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act. The other Acts deal with the press, the movement of plantation workers and equal wages.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which of the following groups contains only rabi crops?
questions.sol: Rabi crops are sown in winter (October to December) and harvested in summer (April to June): wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. Option A and D are kharif crops; option B lists zaid crops.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which one of the following statements about coal in India is correct?
options: The major resources of Gondwana coal are located in the Damodar valley.
Tertiary coal is found mainly in the Damodar valley.
Lignite deposits are found mainly in the north-eastern states.
Lignite is the main coal used in the metallurgical industry.
questions.sol: The major Gondwana coal resources (metallurgical coal) are in the Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro). Tertiary coal occurs in the north-eastern states, lignite is found mainly at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, and high-grade bituminous coal is used in the metallurgical industry.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: A crop grows well on well-drained fertile soils in the flood plains, where the soils are renewed every year, and needs high temperature during the time of its growth. It is used to make gunny bags, mats and ropes. Identify the crop.
questions.sol: Jute, the golden fibre, grows well on well-drained fertile soils in the flood plains where soils are renewed every year, and needs high temperature during growth (West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya). Cotton grows in the drier parts of the black soil of the Deccan plateau; rubber needs rainfall above 200 cm; wheat is a rabi crop of cool growing seasons.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
In the following question, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the appropriate answer from the options given below as the correct answer:
Assertion (A): Jawaharlal Nehru proudly called dams the 'temples of modern India'.
Reason (R): Damming of rivers has led to excessive sedimentation at the bottom of reservoirs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.sol: Both statements are true. Nehru called dams temples of modern India because they would integrate development of agriculture and the village economy with industrialisation. Sedimentation is a problem caused by dams and does not explain why Nehru praised them.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Give two examples to show how the traditional beliefs and practices of communities in India have helped to protect forests and wildlife.
questions.model:
1. Nature worship: sacred groves, the forests of God and Goddesses, have been left untouched by local people and so survive in a virgin form. The Mundas and Santhals of Chota Nagpur worship mahua and kadamba trees, and the tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship tamarind and mango trees during weddings; peepal and banyan trees are considered sacred.
2. In and around Bishnoi villages in Rajasthan, herds of blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks are seen as part of the community and nobody harms them. Many people also protect monkeys such as macaques and langurs around temples.

points.t: First example, e.g. sacred groves left untouched, or worship of trees such as mahua, kadamba, tamarind, mango, peepal, banyan
Second example (different), e.g. Bishnoi villages protecting blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks, or protection of monkeys around temples

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain any three types of pollution caused by manufacturing industries. Suggest two measures to reduce industrial pollution. (3 + 2 = 5)
questions.model:
Types of pollution (any three):
1. Air pollution: a high proportion of undesirable gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide, and smoke from chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants, harm people, animals, plants and buildings.
2. Water pollution: organic and inorganic effluents from paper, pulp, chemical, textile and dyeing industries, petroleum refineries, tanneries and electroplating units are discharged into rivers.
3. Thermal pollution: hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling, harming aquatic life.
4. Noise pollution: noise from industrial machines, generators and saws causes irritation, hearing loss, higher heart rate and blood pressure.
Measures (any two):
1. Reuse and recycle water in two or more stages, and harvest rainwater.
2. Treat hot water and effluents before releasing them into rivers and ponds (primary, secondary and tertiary treatment).
3. Fit smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators; use oil or gas instead of coal.
4. Redesign machinery to be energy-efficient and less noisy, use noise-absorbing material and ear plugs.

points.t: First type of pollution correctly explained (air, water, thermal or noise)
Second type of pollution correctly explained (different from the first)
Third type of pollution correctly explained (different from the first two)
First measure, e.g. treating effluents and hot water before release, or reusing/recycling water
Second measure (different), e.g. electrostatic precipitators/scrubbers on smoke stacks, oil or gas instead of coal, or less noisy machinery

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
The soil of the Deccan lava region
Over large parts of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, the land is covered by a dark soil called regur. The region was once flooded by lava, and the soil has formed from this rock under the climate of the area. The soil is made of extremely fine, clayey material and holds moisture well. It is rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime but generally poor in phosphorus. In the hot season the soil develops deep cracks, which let air into it. When wet, it becomes very sticky. Farmers here have learnt from experience to plan their work around these features.

parts.q: 18.1 Using the information in the text, give one reason why this soil is well suited to growing cotton.
parts.model: It is made of fine clayey material that holds moisture well, so a crop that needs light rainfall gets moisture for a long time; it is also rich in nutrients such as calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. (NCERT: black soil is ideal for growing cotton and is also called black cotton soil.)

points.t: Any one reason from the text: holds moisture well, or rich in nutrients (calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash, lime)

parts.q: 18.2 Explain two features of this soil that a farmer must keep in mind while working on it.
parts.model:
1. It is sticky when wet and difficult to work on, so it must be tilled immediately after the first shower or during the pre-monsoon period.
2. It is generally poor in phosphorus, so the farmer has to add phosphate fertilisers or manure to keep it productive.
(Deep cracks in the hot season help in the aeration of the soil: also acceptable.)

points.t: Sticky when wet, so it must be tilled right after the first shower or in the pre-monsoon period
Poor in phosphorus, so phosphate fertilisers/manure are needed (or deep cracks in summer help aeration)

parts.q: 18.3 Name the two important factors in the formation of this soil.
parts.model: Climatic conditions along with the parent rock material (lava flows of the Deccan trap, basalt).

points.t: Climatic conditions and the parent rock material (lava / basalt)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
In the following question, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the appropriate answer from the options given below as the correct answer:
Assertion (A): A one-party system gives voters a meaningful choice in elections.
Reason (R): In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.sol: A is false: in a one-party system voters have no free choice, so it is not a democratic option. R is true: in China only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which of the following subjects is included in the Concurrent List?
questions.sol: Education is in the Concurrent List, along with forests, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession. Defence and banking are in the Union List; police is in the State List.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about Belgium are correct?
a. The Dutch-speaking community is in the majority in the country as a whole.
b. In the capital city, Brussels, French-speaking people are in the majority.
c. About one per cent of Belgians speak German.
d. Dutch-speaking and French-speaking ministers in the central government are in the ratio of their population.
Choose the correct option:
questions.sol: In Belgium about 59 per cent speak Dutch, 40 per cent French and 1 per cent German; in Brussels about 80 per cent speak French. The Constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch-speaking and French-speaking ministers in the central government shall be equal, so d is wrong.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Why do democracies often take more time to make decisions than non-democratic governments?
options: They follow procedures based on deliberation and negotiation.
They do not allow citizens to take part in decision-making.
They do not hold elections at regular intervals.
They allow only one party to take all decisions.
questions.sol: Democracy is based on deliberation and negotiation, and decisions follow rules and procedures, so some delay is bound to take place. In return, decisions are more acceptable to the people and more effective.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain any two forms that communalism can take in politics.
questions.model:
1. In everyday beliefs: religious prejudices, stereotypes of religious communities and the belief that one's religion is superior to others.
2. A desire for political dominance of one's own religious community: for majority communities this takes the form of majoritarian dominance; for minority communities it can take the form of a desire to form a separate political unit.
3. Political mobilisation on religious lines: using sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and fear to bring the followers of one religion together in politics.
4. Communal violence, riots and massacre, as happened at the time of the Partition.

points.t: First form explained, e.g. religious prejudices and stereotypes in everyday beliefs
Second form explained, e.g. majoritarian dominance/separate political unit, mobilisation on religious lines, or communal violence

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: How has the language policy of the Indian federation helped to strengthen national unity? Give two points.
questions.model:
1. The Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language. Hindi was identified as the official language, and besides Hindi there are 21 other languages recognised as Scheduled Languages; a candidate in a Central Government examination may take the examination in any of these languages, and States have their own official languages.
2. Hindi was not imposed on States where it is not spoken. The use of English along with Hindi for official purposes continued after 1965 because many non-Hindi speaking States demanded it. This careful approach avoided the kind of conflict seen in Sri Lanka.

points.t: No single national language; Hindi as official language along with 21 other Scheduled Languages / States' own official languages
Hindi not imposed on non-Hindi States; English continued alongside Hindi after 1965

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: 'Democracy stands much superior to any other form of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual.' Support the statement with three points.
questions.model:
1. Every individual wants to receive respect from fellow beings. Democracy recognises this and gives citizens rights and freedoms that are protected by law.
2. The long struggles of women have created some sensitivity that respect and equal treatment of women are necessary ingredients of a democratic society; women now have a legal and moral basis to struggle against discrimination.
3. Democracy has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity; untouchability is illegal.
4. People in a democracy keep expecting more and complain about its failings. This itself shows that they have become conscious of their dignity and freedom, and are able to examine those in power.

points.t: First point explained, e.g. democracy gives every individual respect and legally protected rights and freedoms
Second point explained, e.g. women's struggles have made equal treatment of women a necessary part of a democratic society
Third point explained, e.g. claims of disadvantaged castes for equal status, or rising expectations showing awareness of dignity

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain any four elements of the Belgian model of accommodation. Why did this model work better than the approach taken in Sri Lanka? (4 + 1 = 5)
questions.model:
Elements of the Belgian model (any four):
1. The Constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch-speaking and French-speaking ministers in the central government shall be equal, so no single community can make decisions unilaterally.
2. Many powers of the central government have been given to the state governments of the two regions; the state governments are not subordinate to the central government.
3. Brussels has a separate government in which both communities have equal representation.
4. A third kind of government, the community government, is elected by people belonging to one language community (Dutch, French or German-speaking) and has power over cultural, educational and language-related issues.
5. Special laws require the support of a majority of members from each linguistic group.
Why it worked better: Belgium shared power and accommodated the interests of all communities, which helped avoid civic strife and a division of the country on linguistic lines. Sri Lanka followed majoritarian measures that favoured the Sinhala majority; this alienated the Tamils and led to a long civil war.

points.t: First element, e.g. equal number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers in the central government
Second element, e.g. powers given to the state governments of the two regions, not subordinate to the Centre
Third element, e.g. separate government for Brussels with equal representation of both communities
Fourth element, e.g. community government for cultural, educational and language issues, or special laws needing majority support of each linguistic group
Comparison: accommodation in Belgium avoided conflict and division, while majoritarianism in Sri Lanka alienated Tamils and led to civil war

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
Cleaning up party politics
Citizens often complain that political parties do not work democratically within their own organisations and that some candidates use money and muscle power to win elections. Some steps have been taken in recent years. Elected representatives used to leave the party on whose ticket they had won and join another, often for the lure of a ministerial post or money. The Constitution was amended to stop this practice. The Supreme Court has also made it compulsory for every candidate who contests an election to file an affidavit, and the Election Commission has issued an order requiring political parties to hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns. Many people feel that these steps are not enough.

parts.q: 28.1 What is meant by 'defection' in politics?
parts.model: Defection means changing party allegiance from the party on whose ticket a person got elected (to a legislative body) to a different party.

points.t: Changing party allegiance from the party on which one was elected to another party

parts.q: 28.2 Explain how the affidavit ordered by the Supreme Court and the order of the Election Commission can help to improve party politics.
parts.model:
1. The affidavit gives details of the candidate's property and of criminal cases pending against the candidate. This information is made public, so voters can make an informed choice, which reduces the influence of money and crime.
2. The Election Commission's order makes parties hold regular organisational elections and file income tax returns, which encourages internal democracy and makes party finances more transparent.

points.t: Affidavit gives public details of property and pending criminal cases, helping voters judge candidates
EC order: organisational elections and income tax returns promote internal democracy and financial transparency

parts.q: 28.3 Suggest one more reform that could strengthen democracy within political parties.
parts.model: Any one: a law to regulate the internal affairs of parties (keeping a register of members, following their own constitution, an independent authority to act as judge in disputes, open elections to the highest posts); giving a minimum number of tickets, about one-third, to women; state funding of elections; or pressure from people and the media on parties to reform.

points.t: Any one valid reform, e.g. law to regulate internal affairs, one-third tickets to women, state funding of elections

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) of a country indicates:
options: the proportion of children aged 15-17 years attending school
the proportion of literate people aged 7 years and above
the number of children who die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that year
the average number of years a newborn child is expected to live
questions.sol: IMR is the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that particular year. Option A is the net attendance ratio, B is the literacy rate and D is life expectancy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of the public sector?
options: Tata Iron and Steel Company Limited
questions.sol: In the public sector the government owns most of the assets and provides all the services. Indian Railways and the post office are examples; TISCO and Reliance Industries are privately owned.
questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Why are demand deposits with banks considered a form of money?
options: They are printed and issued by the Reserve Bank of India.
They can be withdrawn on demand and are widely accepted for payments by cheque.
They always earn a very high rate of interest for the depositors.
They can be used only for buying assets such as gold and land.
questions.sol: Deposits can be withdrawn on demand, and the cheque facility lets people settle payments directly without cash. Since demand deposits are widely accepted as a means of payment along with currency, they are a form of money. Currency, not deposits, is issued by the RBI.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Farida takes a loan from a bank to buy a house. The bank keeps the papers of the house until the loan is repaid. The house papers here are an example of:
questions.sol: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, a building or a vehicle) and uses as a guarantee to the lender until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell it.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which of the following has greatly reduced port handling costs and increased the speed with which exports reach markets?
options: Use of containers for transport of goods
questions.sol: Goods are placed in containers that can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, aeroplanes and trucks. This has led to a huge reduction in port handling costs and faster movement of exports. The other options restrict trade.
questions.chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
In the following question, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the appropriate answer from the options given below as the correct answer:
Assertion (A): Workers in the unorganised sector often do not get paid leave, holidays or medical benefits.
Reason (R): The unorganised sector is made up of small and scattered units that are largely outside the control of the government.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.sol: Both statements are true. Because these units are largely outside government control, rules and regulations exist but are often not followed, so workers do not get paid leave, holidays or medical benefits. R explains A.
questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA) was replaced in 2025 by the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Viksit Bharat-G RAM G 2025). Explain three provisions of MGNREGA 2005 that aimed to reduce unemployment in rural areas.
questions.model:
1. All those in rural areas who were able to work and were in need of work were guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year by the government.
2. If the government failed in its duty to provide employment, it had to give unemployment allowances to the people.
3. Preference was given to the types of work that would help to increase production from land in future, so the work also created further employment and income in villages.

points.t: Guarantee of 100 days of employment a year to those in rural areas able to and in need of work
Unemployment allowance if the government failed to provide work
Preference to work that would increase production from land in future

questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Ramesh, a small farmer, borrows ₹20,000 from a moneylender at 3 per cent interest per month to buy seeds and fertilisers.
(a) How much interest (simple interest) will he have to pay for one year? (1)
(b) How can such a loan push him into a debt trap? (1)
(c) Suggest one cheaper source of credit for him and say why it is better. (1)
questions.model:
(a) Interest for one year = ₹20,000 x 3/100 x 12 = ₹600 x 12 = ₹7,200 (that is, 36 per cent per year).
(b) If the crop fails or prices are low, his earnings may not be enough to repay the loan with such high interest. He then has to sell part of his land or take a fresh loan to repay the old one, so his debt keeps growing. This situation is called a debt trap.
(c) A bank or a cooperative society (or a self-help group). Formal lenders charge much lower rates of interest and are supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, so he will not be exploited.

points.t: (b) Crop failure/low earnings leave him unable to repay, so he borrows again or sells land and his debt keeps growing
(c) Bank, cooperative or SHG, with a reason: lower interest / supervised by RBI

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: A garment company in Delhi designs clothes, gets them stitched by a factory in Tiruppur, Tamil Nadu, and sells them to a buyer in London. Explain three ways in which information and communication technology makes this possible.
questions.model:
1. Telecommunication facilities (telephone, mobile phones, fax) are used to contact others around the world, to place orders and to access information instantly at low cost.
2. Designs can be prepared on a computer and sent by e-mail over the internet to the factory in Tiruppur and to the buyer in London within seconds, and changes can be agreed quickly.
3. Payment can be made instantly from a bank in London to a bank in Delhi through the internet (e-banking), and people can talk (voice-mail) across the world at negligible cost.

points.t: Telecommunication (telephone, mobile, fax) for instant contact and ordering at low cost
Computers and the internet (e-mail) to send designs and information instantly
E-banking (payment through the internet) or voice-mail at negligible cost across countries

questions.chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Study the table given below and answer the questions that follow.
Monthly incomes of the five citizens of two countries (in ₹, imaginary data)
CountryCitizen ICitizen IICitizen IIICitizen IVCitizen V
P11,80012,40011,60012,00012,200
Q1,0001,5001,0001,50055,000
(a) Calculate the average monthly income of the citizens of each country. (1)
(b) In which country would you prefer to live? Give two reasons. (2)
(c) What limitation of the average income does this example show? Name one other indicator that should be used to compare the development of the two countries. (2)
questions.model:
(a) Country P: (11,800 + 12,400 + 11,600 + 12,000 + 12,200) / 5 = 60,000 / 5 = ₹12,000.
Country Q: (1,000 + 1,500 + 1,000 + 1,500 + 55,000) / 5 = 60,000 / 5 = ₹12,000.
(b) Country P. 1. Incomes are distributed fairly equally, so every citizen earns close to the average. 2. In Country Q, four out of five citizens earn only ₹1,000-1,500 a month and are poor; one person is extremely rich.
(c) The average is useful for comparison, but it hides the disparities (the distribution of income) among people. Two countries with the same average income can have very different levels of well-being. Other indicators such as the infant mortality rate, literacy rate, net attendance ratio, life expectancy or the Human Development Index should also be used.

points.t: (a) Average income of both P and Q is ₹12,000
(b) Country P, because incomes are distributed equally / everyone earns close to the average
(b) In Q, most citizens are poor and one person is very rich (unequal distribution)
(c) The average hides disparities in the distribution of income among people
(c) One other indicator, e.g. IMR, literacy rate, net attendance ratio, life expectancy or HDI
